title: Pair That Hits the Target
ask: Find two different positions whose numbers add up to the target.
given: A list of numbers, and a target number.
returns: The two indexes, smaller one first.
story: The question is not asking you to invent new numbers. It is asking where a pair sits. Checking every pair works, and it is slow. As you walk from left to right, remember each number you have already seen. For the number in your hand, ask one question: have I already seen the missing piece?

steps.title: Start with 2
steps.body: The list is [2, 7, 11, 15] and the target is 9. The first number is 2, so the missing piece is 7. You have not seen 7 yet. Remember that 2 sits at index 0.

steps.title: Next number is 7
steps.body: 7 needs 2 to make 9. You remembered 2 at index 0. That pair is the answer: indexes 0 and 1.

steps.title: Why this is enough
steps.body: You never look backward through the whole list. The memory of earlier numbers answers the question in one step.

hint: Keep a map of numbers you have passed. Before you save the current number, check whether target minus that number is already in the map.

title: Balanced Gates
ask: Decide whether every gate that opens is closed in the right order.
returns: true when the string is balanced, otherwise false.
story: Read the string from left to right. An opening bracket is a gate you walk through. The last gate you opened has to be the next one that closes. A pile works for that: put openings on top, and a closing bracket must match whatever is currently on top.

steps.title: Open, then close
steps.body: For (), you place ( on the pile, then ) matches it and you take it off. The pile is empty, so this string is balanced.

steps.title: Wrong closer
steps.body: For (], you place ( on the pile. ] does not match (. The string is not balanced.

steps.title: Nested gates
steps.body: For {[]}, the pile grows as { then [, then ] closes [, then } closes {. Empty pile at the end means yes.

hint: Push opening brackets. When you see a closer, it must equal the matching opener you just popped.

examples.why: Each opener has the right closer.
A round gate is closed by a square one.

title: Stair Steps
ask: Count the ways to climb a staircase when each move is 1 step or 2 steps.
returns: How many different ways reach the top.
story: To stand on step n, the last move came from step n-1 (a single step) or step n-2 (a double step). So the ways to reach n are the ways to reach n-1 plus the ways to reach n-2. That is the whole problem. You do not need to list every path.

steps.title: Two steps
steps.body: You can climb 1 then 1, or one double step. That is 2 ways.

steps.title: Three steps
steps.body: 1+1+1, 1+2, and 2+1. That is 3 ways. 2+1 and 1+2 are different orders, so both count.

steps.title: The pattern
steps.body: Each new step adds the two numbers before it: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. Step 5 has 8 ways.

pattern: Build the answer from the two smaller stairs.
hint: Keep only the last two totals as you walk from step 3 up to n.

title: Longest Unique Stretch
ask: Find the longest stretch of the text that never repeats a character.
returns: The length of that stretch, not the stretch itself.
story: Imagine a window on the string. The right edge moves forward one character at a time. If that character is already inside the window, slide the left edge forward until the repeat is gone. The window is always a stretch with unique characters. Remember the biggest width you saw.

steps.title: abcabcbb
steps.body: The window grows across a, b, c. Width 3. The next a is already inside, so the left edge moves past the first a.

steps.title: Keep sliding
steps.body: b, c, a is still width 3. Later repeats never beat that width. The answer is 3.

steps.title: All the same
steps.body: bbbbb never holds more than one unique character, so the answer is 1.

hint: Store the last index of each character. When you repeat one, jump the left edge to just after its previous index.

title: Same Letters
ask: Group words that use exactly the same letters.
returns: Groups of words. Sort each group alphabetically, then sort the groups by their first word.
story: eat, tea, and ate are the same letters in different order. If you sort the letters inside a word, those three all become aet. That sorted string is a label. Words with the same label belong in the same group.

steps.title: Label each word
steps.body: eat, tea, and ate all sort into aet. tan and nat sort into ant. bat stays abt.

steps.title: Drop words into buckets
steps.body: One bucket for aet, one for ant, one for abt.

steps.title: Make the answer stable
steps.body: Sort inside each bucket, then sort the buckets by the first word. The reader can compare answers without caring who found a group first.

pattern: Hash map, keyed by the word's letters in order.
hint: Sort the characters of each word and use that string as the map key.

examples.why: eat, tea, and ate share their letters. So do tan and nat. bat is alone.
